title: Backward Through the Network: How to Run U.S. Returns Freight This January
summary: U.S. holiday returns freight runs backward through networks built for outbound. How to handle appointments, OS&D, detention and billing into January 2027.
body_markdown:
The tender hits at 4:40 p.m. on the Friday after Christmas. A retailer's 3PL wants 14 truckloads of returns moved from three return centers to a liquidator two states away. The load notes say "mixed general merchandise, floor loaded and palletized, approx. 22 pallets."


There's no appointment at the consignee. There's no piece count. The shipper of record is a building your team has never served.


You take it anyway. The miles look like a decent backhaul.


On Monday, the first driver waits seven hours at the liquidator and gets turned away because the dock is already full.


The receiver later writes "12 pallets damaged, wrapping broken" on a delivery receipt. The freight left the origin looking exactly that way.


The story is made up. The pattern is not. Every January, freight built to flow outward, from import DC to store or doorstep, starts running backward.


It moves through buildings, labor plans and billing rules that were never designed for it. If you don't change how you tender, price and document those loads, January will take the margin December earned.


## The volume coming back at you


Per the national retail trade association's October forecast, released Oct. 15, 2026, November and December retail sales should grow 4.2% over 2025, to about $1.013 trillion. That's after a 3.1% gain last season, to $972 billion.


Returns follow that curve. The same group's 2025 returns report came out in October 2025, with a returns technology partner. Retailers expected 15.8% of annual sales to come back, about $849.9 billion.


That's down from 16.9% and $890 billion in 2024, but it's still a huge reverse flow. Online sales ran hotter, with an estimated 19.3% returned. Retailers expected 17% of holiday sales to be returned, "consistent with previous years."


No 2026 edition was out at the time of writing. Treat those figures as the latest benchmark, not a fresh forecast.


Apply that 17% holiday rate to this year's sales forecast and you get roughly $170 billion of merchandise coming back.


A lot of it goes back to shelves through stores. The share bound for return centers, liquidators and recyclers still moves in truckload and LTL lanes during the weakest outbound weeks of the year.


Retailers planned to lean more on third-party logistics partners (49%), hire seasonal returns staff (43%) and extend return windows (37%). Those longer windows stretch the wave into February. More 3PL tenders often come from a party that doesn't control the receiving dock.


The same publisher found 60% of retailers had, at some point, been forced to choose between shipping new orders and processing returns. That's the labor conflict you feel as a missed appointment and a driver sitting on the yard.


## The market you'll be moving it in


This year's backward flow arrives in a tighter market than the last three Januaries.


A freight payment index report for October 2026 showed shipments up 5.9% year over year. That's the third straight annual gain after a long run of declines, so the market has been tightening for months.


Expenditures were up 26.5%, and the truckload linehaul index was up 9.9%. The report tied the spend surge to higher shipments, rates and fuel surcharges. It projected expenditures up about 24% year over year in November under normal seasonality.


More freight is moving, and it costs more to move it.


The building side is tight too. A university-led logistics managers' survey for October 2026, released Nov. 3, put the overall index at 70.7. That's the second-highest reading since March 2022, so activity is running hot.


Warehousing capacity read 43.5, which means space is still contracting. Warehousing prices sat at 80.7. Transportation capacity read 38.0, its eleventh straight month of contraction. Transportation prices sat at 88.0.


Downstream retail respondents were building inventory faster than upstream firms, a sign of holiday stocking. Inventory costs hit their highest reading since March 2022.


January looks different from 2024 and 2025. Buildings already full of holiday stock have less room for returns, and carriers have better outbound options than a year ago. Price a returns lane like last January and you're leaving money on the table, or parking a truck where it can't earn.


## Where January goes wrong


The failures start with the tender.


**Tendered without an appointment.** Returns loads are often booked by someone who doesn't own the receiving dock. The 3PL or retailer tenders, the liquidator or processor receives, and nobody confirms a slot.


You end up in a first-come-first-served line at a building that's short-staffed after the holidays. Block dispatch until a consignee appointment or confirmed receiving window is on the load. You'll lose a few tenders and save far more in detention you can't collect.


**Unknown or mixed-condition freight.** A returns pallet is not an outbound pallet. Counts are approximate, packaging is already open, and some product is damaged before you ever hook to the trailer. If you accept "said to contain" freight with a vague piece count, you're accepting a claim fight later.


**Condition ownership at pickup.** On outbound freight, a clean bill of lading means something. On returns, the condition at origin is the whole question.


If your driver can't inspect shrink-wrapped mixed pallets, the bill of lading should say so. Note shipper load and count, condition unknown, and exceptions with photos.


Without that record, a receiver's damage notation shifts the presumption onto you. Pickup photos and exception notes should be required fields in your OS&D workflow, not optional attachments.


**Detention at returns centers and liquidators.** These buildings sort, grade and reprocess, and that work competes with unloading for the same labor. If your rate confirmation skips free time, detention rates or the paperwork you need to bill them, you'll eat the hours.


**Accessorials nobody quoted.** Returns also bring charges nobody put on the quote. Think lumper fees, sort and segregate, pallet exchange, restack, disposal of damaged goods, and a trailer wash after a spill.


On many of these lanes, the shipper and the payer are different parties. A lumper receipt in the driver's hand may not match who you can actually invoice.


## Who actually owns the problem


Visibility breaks along the same lines as responsibility. The retailer watches recovery value, the 3PL watches building space, and the broker watches whether the invoice clears.


You want the truck loaded again. Each party sees its own slice, and the load falls through the gap.


**Asset carriers** usually want returns lanes as backhaul. That's a good deal when the returns center sits near an outbound delivery and the consignee will take a timed appointment. It's a bad deal when the load strands a tractor at a liquidator for a day in a tight outbound week.


Price the return as a standalone move first. Then decide how much to give back for network balance. You can't do that math without true dwell history per facility.


**Brokers** live with the mismatch. The shops that do well in January track facility-level dwell and claims history and attach that to the quote. A returns center with seven-hour waits needs a different rate than one that turns trucks in two hours. It also needs a stricter detention clause.


**Hybrid shops** have the most options and the most room for confusion. When an asset division and a brokerage desk both touch the same returns account, they need one view of the customer's accessorial terms. They need one set of OS&D rules, and one answer about who owns a claim.


Otherwise the asset side absorbs losses the brokerage side already quoted away.


## How to price it without giving the lane away


Returns consolidation looks like cheap capacity on paper. A few practices make it work.


-


**Price the dwell, not just the miles.** Build expected dwell per facility into the rate. Don't lean on detention billing you may never collect.


-


**Quote accessorials by default.** List sort, disposal, lumper and restack as named line items with rates on the rate confirmation, even if they rarely apply. A charge that was quoted is a charge you can bill.


-


**Separate consolidation stops cleanly.** Multi-stop returns pickups should carry per-stop piece counts and condition notes. Then a damage dispute at delivery can be traced to the stop where it started.


-


**Set a floor.** If a returns lane only works as backhaul at a rate below your cost of moving the truck empty, it isn't a lane. It's a subsidy.


## What changed at the border


Duty-free treatment for low-value imports ended on Aug. 29, 2025. U.S. Customs and Border Protection applied that change to shipments entered on or after that date, regardless of value or country of origin. Non-postal shipments now need a formal entry.


For retailers and brands with foreign return addresses or cross-border fulfillment, that changed the cost of where returns get processed. Sending low-value goods back across the border now carries entry work and possible duties it didn't carry two seasons ago.


For domestic operators, the likely effect is more returns processing kept inside the U.S. You'll also see more customers asking you to hold, sort or stage goods. That's more dwell, more handling and more accessorial work in a month that already runs hot.


## What to do before the first January tender


1.


**Write a returns tender rule.** No dispatch without a consignee appointment or confirmed receiving hours, a stated pallet or piece range, and a named payer for accessorials.


2.


**Make pickup condition evidence mandatory.** Photos, seal numbers and exception notes on every returns pickup, captured in the same record as the load. Claims staff shouldn't have to chase drivers for them in February.


3.


**Pull facility dwell history.** Rank the returns centers and liquidators you served last January by average dwell and refusal rate. Use it to price, to set free time, and to decline the worst offenders.


4.


**Align the accessorial schedule with the customer contract.** Confirm who pays lumper, sort and disposal on each returns account before peak returns season, not after the first invoice is short-paid.


5.


**Separate returns freight in your reporting.** If returns loads share a status and a service type with outbound freight, you'll never see their real margin or claims rate.


## Make your system match the freight


No two returns programs look the same. One shipper's returns are high-value electronics that need serial-level counts and secure trailers. Another's are bulky home goods headed for disposal, where the risk is a refused load. A third mixes both on the same pallet.


The operators who handle January well are rarely the cheapest. They're the ones whose systems reflect how their freight actually behaves.


Tender rules that require an appointment for specific consignees. Statuses that distinguish a returns pickup from an outbound one. Permissions that keep a broker from quoting away an asset division's detention terms. Billing rules that know which accessorials belong to which customer. Capacity logic that knows when a backhaul is worth taking.


That configuration work is unglamorous. But it's where a network built for outbound learns to run backward without losing money.


## FAQ


### How much holiday merchandise do U.S. retailers expect to be returned?


Retailers expected about 17% of holiday sales to be returned, per the national retail trade association's 2025 returns report. It estimated 15.8% of total 2025 sales, about $849.9 billion, would come back. No 2026 edition was out at the time of writing.


### When does returns freight peak after the holidays?


Returns freight typically builds through late December and January, and longer return windows stretch it into February. The 2025 returns report found 37% of retailers planned to extend those windows.


### Who is responsible for damage on returned goods picked up by a carrier?


Responsibility usually depends on what the bill of lading and pickup records show about condition at origin. When mixed returns pallets can't be inspected, note shipper load and count and record exceptions with photos, or a receiver's damage notation can shift the presumption onto you.


### Is returns freight good backhaul for asset carriers?


It can be, but only when dwell is predictable and the rate covers the time the truck actually spends there. Price it from facility-level dwell history, not miles alone.


### Did the end of de minimis change how returns are handled?


Yes. Duty-free treatment for low-value imports ended on Aug. 29, 2025, so low-value goods returned into the U.S. can now face entry requirements and potential duties.
